questions.q: What does Jon Acuff say about waiting to discover your purpose?
a: You should stop waiting and give purpose to what you do now
You should keep searching until the right calling appears
You should copy the purpose of someone you admire
You should only start once you have a ten-year plan
questions.why: Lesson 1 says not having a purpose becomes an excuse for doing nothing, so you should live with purpose today.

questions.q: How does the summary suggest treating your life while you explore interests?
a: As a series of experiments that produce useful data
As a single path you must commit to for life
As a competition against more successful people
As a test you should only attempt once
questions.why: Lesson 2 says a failed attempt is just data showing what does not work, so you can run the next experiment.

questions.q: What question does Acuff offer to kickstart the search for what you love?
a: What would you most regret never having done if you died tomorrow?
What could you do better than anyone else you know?
Which career pays the most for the least effort?
What did you enjoy most as a small child?
questions.why: Lesson 2 uses this regret question to point you toward experiences worth trying.

questions.q: What does the summary recommend once you notice which activities you enjoy most?
a: Edit your life to do more of them and less of the rest
Keep every activity so your options stay open
Turn all of them into a single business
Wait until you are an expert before choosing
questions.why: Lesson 3 advises removing the activities you dislike and gradually doubling down on the ones you love.

questions.q: Why should the editing of your life happen slowly?
a: It is an incremental process of removing and adding in small steps
Big changes are impossible without professional help
You need permission from your employer first
Your interests will disappear if you act too fast
questions.why: Lesson 3 says to make each edit in increments and move on only when the time feels right.
